title: Vasculitis Testing: PR3/MPO-ANCA, Fixation Artefacts and Cryoglobulins
summary: Use antigen-specific PR3 and MPO immunoassays first, understand why ethanol-fixed P-ANCA can be an artefact and how formalin helps, recognize atypical ANCA, and keep cryoglobulin samples warm.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 54 Hits 1, 2, 3, 5 and 9 and Traps 1, 3 and 6 (first lesson for Ch. 54). Checked against Kozmar 2025 (national recommendations following the 2017 consensus; the Bossuyt 2017 position paper itself was not read), Can 2026 and Kolopp-Sarda 2020. Not taught as fact: “pauci-immune” immunofluorescence, anti-GBM, PAN, GCA, Kawasaki, HUV/anti-C1q, HBV–PAN, EGPA phenotypes, rheumatoid vasculitis, Takayasu, dual MPO+PR3 positivity in drug-induced AAV, the 11–17%/9–16% seronegativity figures, the 3–7-day incubation range and the “>80% HCV” figure.

objectives: Name the two clinically relevant ANCA targets and their main disease associations.
Explain the ethanol-fixation P-ANCA artefact, the role of formalin, and atypical ANCA.
Apply the antigen-first ANCA algorithm and the warm-handling rule for cryoglobulins.

scenes.title: A perinuclear glow
scenes.altText: Invented case: a 64-year-old has rapidly worsening kidney function and blood in the urine. Indirect immunofluorescence on ETHANOL-fixed neutrophils shows a PERINUCLEAR (P-ANCA-like) pattern. The same patient’s cryoglobulin sample arrived at the laboratory packed on ice. Question token: “Is the perinuclear pattern real MPO-ANCA — and can the cryoglobulin result be trusted?”

cues.text: A 64-year-old has rapidly worsening kidneys and blood in the urine.
On ethanol-fixed neutrophils, the patient’s serum gives a perinuclear glow. And a cryoglobulin sample arrived on ice.
Is the perinuclear pattern true MPO-ANCA, and can the cryoglobulin result be trusted?

scenes.title: Two clinically relevant targets
scenes.altText: Target card (Kozmar 2025): ANCA are autoantibodies to proteins in neutrophil primary granules and monocyte lysosomes; the clinically relevant specificities are proteinase 3 (PR3) and myeloperoxidase (MPO). PR3- or MPO-ANCA are a hallmark of ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV), a small-vessel vasculitis: granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) mostly PR3-ANCA; microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) mostly MPO-ANCA; eosinophilic GPA ANCA-positive in ~50%, mostly MPO. Pattern card: historically, IIF on ethanol-fixed granulocytes shows cytoplasmic (C-ANCA, mostly PR3) or perinuclear (P-ANCA, mostly MPO) staining; other patterns are “atypical”. Schematic neutrophils.

cues.text: ANCA are autoantibodies against proteins in neutrophil granules. Only two targets are clinically relevant: proteinase 3 and myeloperoxidase.
They mark ANCA-associated vasculitis, a small-vessel disease. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is mostly PR3-ANCA; microscopic polyangiitis is mostly MPO-ANCA.
On ethanol-fixed neutrophils, PR3 antibodies usually give a granular cytoplasmic pattern, C-ANCA; MPO antibodies usually give a perinuclear pattern, P-ANCA.
Anything else is called atypical ANCA.

scenes.title: Why the perinuclear pattern can lie
scenes.altText: Fixation card (Can 2026): ethanol fixation can redistribute cytoplasmic antigens toward the nucleus, generating ARTIFACTUAL perinuclear staining; formalin fixation preserves cytoplasmic localization. In 7,276 patients tested on both substrates, formalin-RESISTANT P-ANCA had a markedly higher rate of MPO positivity, whereas MPO positivity was uncommon in formalin-SENSITIVE patterns. Look-alike card (Kozmar 2025): atypical P-ANCA without well-characterized specificity occurs in inflammatory bowel disease (40–70% of ulcerative colitis) and autoimmune liver diseases; drug-induced AAV (e.g. hydralazine, propylthiouracil, minocycline, anti-TNF) is mostly high-titre MPO-ANCA with coexisting antinuclear antibodies.

cues.text: Ethanol fixation can let cytoplasmic proteins drift toward the nucleus, so a perinuclear pattern on ethanol can be an artefact.
Formalin holds cytoplasmic proteins in place. In over seven thousand patients, P-ANCA that persisted on formalin was much more often MPO-positive; patterns that vanished on formalin rarely were.
Atypical perinuclear ANCA without a defined target is common in ulcerative colitis, 40 to 70 percent of patients, and in autoimmune liver disease. That is not vasculitis.
And drugs such as hydralazine, propylthiouracil or minocycline can trigger vasculitis with high-titre MPO-ANCA, often alongside antinuclear antibodies.

scenes.title: The modern algorithm and the warm cryoglobulin
scenes.altText: Algorithm card (Kozmar 2025, following the revised 2017 international consensus): if AAV is suspected, use high-quality antigen-specific PR3-ANCA and MPO-ANCA immunoassays as the PRIMARY screen; if negative but clinical suspicion is strong — or if weakly positive — add IIF on ethanol-fixed (preferably plus formalin-fixed) granulocytes and/or an alternative high-quality immunoassay; if the referral diagnosis is unknown, IIF can screen, and any positive or cytoplasmic fluorescence must be followed by PR3/MPO immunoassays. Cryoglobulin card (Kolopp-Sarda 2020): cryoglobulins precipitate in the cold and dissolve at 37 °C. Method: clot at 37 °C (2 h) to avoid precipitation, centrifuge, store serum at +4 °C for 7 days, then inspect for cryoprecipitate. Types: I monoclonal Ig; II monoclonal Ig with rheumatoid-factor activity bound to polyclonal IgG; III polyclonal (II and III = mixed). Hook answers: confirm with MPO immunoassay and formalin IIF; recollect the cryoglobulin warm.

cues.text: Today the first test for suspected ANCA vasculitis is a high-quality antigen-specific immunoassay for PR3 and MPO antibodies.
If those are negative but suspicion is strong, or the result is only weakly positive, add immunofluorescence on ethanol and formalin slides, or a second immunoassay.
Cryoglobulins precipitate in the cold and dissolve at body temperature. So blood must clot at 37 degrees, then the serum is kept at 4 degrees for a week and checked for a precipitate.

For our patient: confirm the perinuclear pattern with an MPO immunoassay and formalin slide, and recollect the cryoglobulin sample warm. Ice before separation can make the cryoglobulin fall out with the clot.

props.label: Hook: MPO assay + formalin IIF · recollect cryo warm

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A P-ANCA pattern means an antibody to the nucleus” (✓ ethanol-fixation artefact can create perinuclear staining — confirm with formalin IIF and an MPO immunoassay); “Atypical P-ANCA means vasculitis” (✓ common in ulcerative colitis and autoimmune liver disease; usually not MPO/PR3); “Send the cryoglobulin sample on ice” (✓ keep at 37 °C until clotted and separated; cold first = false negative).

cues.text: Trap one: P-ANCA means the antibody targets the nucleus. No: ethanol fixation can move cytoplasmic proteins toward the nucleus. Confirm with formalin slides and an MPO immunoassay.
Trap two: an atypical P-ANCA means vasculitis. No: it is common in ulcerative colitis and autoimmune liver disease, usually without PR3 or MPO specificity.
Trap three: send the cryoglobulin on ice. No: keep it at 37 degrees until it has clotted and been separated, or the cryoglobulin is lost.

props.title: ✗ “P-ANCA = anti-nuclear antibody.”
lines: ✓ Fixation artefact possible — formalin + MPO assay

props.title: ✗ “Atypical P-ANCA = vasculitis.”
lines: ✓ UC, autoimmune liver disease; not PR3/MPO

scenes.title: Ethanol lets it wander
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Ethanol lets MPO WANDER to the nucleus; formalin FREEZES it in place. And cryoglobulins are cold-blooded: keep them WARM until you’re ready to chill them on purpose.” Tokens: ethanol = wander · formalin = hold · cryo: 37 °C first, 4 °C later. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: ethanol lets MPO wander to the nucleus; formalin freezes it in place. And cryoglobulins are cold-blooded: keep them warm until you chill them on purpose.

Where it breaks: antinuclear antibodies can also produce a P-ANCA-like reading on ethanol slides, especially at high titre, so an antigen-specific assay is still needed; immunofluorescence must be run at high sensitivity; and no single ANCA assay catches every patient with vasculitis.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Suspected AAV: PR3 + MPO immunoassays first · P-ANCA on ethanol can be artefact → formalin IIF · atypical P-ANCA in UC/liver disease”, “Cryoglobulins: clot at 37 °C, then 4 °C for 7 days · type I monoclonal, II mixed with RF, III polyclonal”.

cues.text: Antigen-specific PR3 and MPO immunoassays now come first for suspected ANCA vasculitis because ethanol-fixed perinuclear patterns can be artefacts or non-vasculitic, and cryoglobulin samples must stay at 37 degrees until the serum is separated.

props.label: PR3 + MPO immunoassays first · ethanol P-ANCA can be artefact
Cryo: clot 37 °C → 4 °C 7 days · I mono · II mixed RF · III poly

explanation.what: Plain language: in some vasculitis the immune system attacks two neutrophil enzymes; tests that measure those enzymes directly are now preferred, because the older microscope test can be fooled by how the slide was fixed. Cryoglobulins are proteins that clump in the cold, so samples must stay warm. Scientific terms: ANCA, proteinase 3, myeloperoxidase, C-ANCA, P-ANCA, atypical ANCA, indirect immunofluorescence, ethanol vs formalin fixation, antigen-specific immunoassay, ANCA-associated vasculitis (GPA, MPA, EGPA), cryoglobulin types I–III.
explanation.why: Ethanol can move cytoplasmic antigens toward the nucleus, so the IIF pattern reflects fixation as well as antibody target; formalin keeps them in place. Antigen-specific assays identify PR3 or MPO directly. Cryoglobulins precipitate below body temperature, so cooling before separation removes them with the clot.
explanation.measure: Primary screen: high-quality PR3- and MPO-ANCA immunoassays; IIF on ethanol + formalin and/or a second immunoassay for negative-but-suspicious or weak results (Kozmar 2025). Formalin-resistant P-ANCA more often MPO+ (Can 2026). Cryoglobulins: clot at 37 °C 2 h, centrifuge, serum at +4 °C 7 days, inspect (Kolopp-Sarda 2020).
explanation.differs: C-ANCA/PR3 (mostly GPA) vs P-ANCA/MPO (mostly MPA); true MPO P-ANCA (formalin-resistant, MPO+) vs ethanol artefact or atypical ANCA (IBD, liver disease); cryoglobulin type I (monoclonal) vs II (monoclonal RF + polyclonal IgG) vs III (polyclonal).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: pick antigen-specific assays as the first ANCA test, explain a P-ANCA artefact or atypical ANCA in ulcerative colitis, and identify mishandled (chilled) cryoglobulin samples.

questions.stem: Under the revised 2017 consensus, what is the primary screening test for suspected ANCA-associated vasculitis?

options.text: High-quality antigen-specific PR3-ANCA and MPO-ANCA immunoassays
options.rationale: Correct. Antigen-specific immunoassays are the primary screen; IIF is added in selected situations.
Incorrect. IIF is no longer required as the first step when AAV is suspected.
Incorrect. ANA does not detect PR3 or MPO antibodies.
Incorrect. Cryoglobulins are a separate vasculitis cause.

questions.stem: A perinuclear pattern seen on ethanol-fixed neutrophils disappears on formalin-fixed neutrophils, and MPO-ANCA is negative. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Likely an ethanol-fixation artefact or atypical ANCA, not MPO-ANCA
options.rationale: Correct. Formalin-sensitive patterns were rarely MPO-positive (Can 2026); the MPO assay is negative.
Incorrect. Both the formalin result and the MPO immunoassay argue against it.
Incorrect. PR3 typically gives cytoplasmic staining and requires a PR3 immunoassay.
Incorrect. Cryoglobulins are not detected by ANCA IIF.

questions.stem: A cryoglobulin specimen is placed in an ice bath immediately after collection. What is the likely effect?

options.text: False-negative result, because cryoglobulins precipitate with the clot before the serum is separated
options.rationale: Correct. Samples must clot at 37 °C so cryoglobulins stay in the serum.
Incorrect. The problem is loss of cryoglobulin from the serum.

options.text: No effect, since the serum is cooled later anyway
options.rationale: Incorrect. Cooling before separation removes the cryoglobulin.

options.text: It converts type III to type I cryoglobulin
options.rationale: Incorrect. Temperature does not change the immunoglobulin composition.
